summary: This informational report from the IRTF Host Identity Protocol research group collects experiences and lessons from studies, experiments, and designs. It summarizes the implications of adding HIP to host stacks, infrastructure, and applications, from an operator's view too.

eli5.summary: A group of researchers tried a new way for computers to identify themselves. This is their write-up of what worked, what was hard, and what they learned.

subtitle: Lessons learned from experimental deployments of the Host Identity Protocol.

tldr.problem: The Internet hardwires IP addresses as both identifiers (who you are) and locators (where you are), making it difficult to support mobility, multihoming, and security without breaking existing connections.
tldr.mechanism: HIP introduces a new namespace called Host Identities, which are cryptographic identifiers independent of IP addresses. Hosts exchange identities using a protocol compatible with the Sigma signature scheme, then use IPsec ESP to protect traffic while IP addresses change.
tldr.outcome: Early implementations and deployments from 2004-2009 revealed practical challenges in kernel modifications, name resolution, firewall interaction, and application compatibility, resulting in recommendations for future HIP evolution.

today: RFC 6538 is an Informational report from the IRTF HIP Research Group, published in March 2012. It documents experimental findings and lessons learned from HIP deployments between 2004 and 2009, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What HIP Does
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) architecture introduces a new namespace called Host Identities, allowing the decoupling of identifiers (who a host is) from locators (where it is). Host Identities are represented as Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers (ORCHIDs), which are public key cryptographic identifiers. HIP also addresses several Internet challenges: host mobility (a device moving between networks), host and site multihoming (using multiple connections), IPv6 transition, NAT traversal, and network-level security.

The HIP protocol itself exchanges host identities (public keys) using a Diffie-Hellman key exchange compliant with Sigma ("SIGn-and-MAc"). When combined with Encapsulated Security Payload (ESP), HIP provides encryption and authentication for upper-layer protocols like TCP and UDP while preserving connection continuity across network-layer address changes.
sections.eli5: HIP gives each computer a permanent identity (like a name) that is separate from its temporary address (like a street address). When the computer moves to a different network, its identity stays the same, so conversations don't break.

sections.title: Implementation Approaches
sections.content:
HIP implementations follow two primary strategies. The first modifies the kernel TCP/IP stack directly to support decoupling of identifiers and locators, offering better data throughput performance but requiring substantial operating system changes. The second implements all HIP processing in user-space, configuring the kernel to route HIP packets through a user-space daemon via a virtual network device (such as a TAP device).

In kernel-based implementations, HIP coordinates with an IPsec-extended stack through a key management process. The process manages security associations and policies, often using the PF_KEY API for communication with the kernel's Security Association Database (SAD) and Security Policy Database (SPD). User-space implementations use packet filtering or routing rules to divert relevant packets to a daemon, which applies ESP headers, replaces HITs with IP addresses, and re-injects packets back into the stack.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to add HIP to a computer: change the deep system parts (the kernel) for speed, or add it as a program that talks to the kernel. Both ways work, but have different trade-offs.

sections.title: HITs, LSIs, and Name Resolution
sections.content:
HIP uses two addressing schemes. Host Identity Tags (HITs) are cryptographic identifiers that fit into the IPv6 address space reserved for ORCHIDs. IPv6 applications can bind directly to HITs. For IPv4 applications, HIP defines Local Scope Identifiers (LSIs), which have significance only within a host; the HIP layer translates from LSIs to IP addresses used for actual packet transmission.

A critical challenge is HIT resolution: how do two hosts discover each other's HITs? Early experimentation relied on manual HIT exchange, which did not scale. Solutions included storing HITs in DNS AAAA records, using distributed hash tables (DHTs) like OpenDHT, or supporting RFC 5205 DNS extensions. Opportunistic mode allows the Initiator to start a base exchange without prior knowledge of the Responder's HIT, eliminating the need for lookup infrastructure but requiring a "leap of faith" about identity until other verification occurs.
sections.eli5: Every computer gets a permanent identity (HIT) that fits in IPv6 space, and older computers get a temporary local address (LSI). Finding another computer's identity is hard, so people tried different ways: storing it in DNS, asking a shared database, or just guessing and checking.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
Infrastructure deployment of HIP requires several new elements. Rendezvous servers help hosts discover and reach each other when they move, registering their current IP address so peers can contact them. HIT-aware middleboxes (firewalls, NAT devices) must understand HIP to permit or filter HIP traffic correctly. DNS extensions (RFC 5205) and HIP-aware DHT services support HIT-to-address resolution.

Network operators face policy challenges: they must decide whether to use access control lists (ACLs) based on HITs (providing host-level control) rather than IP addresses, and how to manage HIP in encrypted ESP tunnels. Firewall interaction is complex because HIP changes the binding between identity and address, potentially breaking stateful packet inspection and connection tracking. The BEET (Bound End-to-End Tunnel) mode used by HIP mixes tunnel and transport semantics, requiring kernel modifications not present in all distributions.
sections.eli5: Network managers need new tools to let HIP computers talk to each other, handle HIT discovery, and make firewall rules that work when addresses change.

sections.title: Application Compatibility and User Experience
sections.content:
Applications do not inherently benefit from HIP unless they are explicitly HIP-aware. Legacy applications using the standard AF_INET and AF_INET6 sockets APIs continue to work, but they do not automatically gain mobility or multihoming support from HIP. HIP-aware applications can detect address changes and adapt behavior, or use referrals in protocols to inform peers of new addresses.

A major usability issue is that manual HIT exchange has been "a major inconvenience for experimentation." Opportunistic mode helps but introduces complexity at the socket layer. Latency is another concern: establishing a HIP base exchange takes time, though extensions have been explored to reduce delays to a single round-trip time. User research on security interfaces ("usable security") suggests that prompting users to explicitly accept new identities can help mitigate "leap of faith" concerns in opportunistic mode.
sections.eli5: Old programs don't automatically work better with HIP. HIP works best when programs are designed for it, but then people have to set it up carefully, and it takes time for connections to start.
